And likewise the soul: He swears by it and by the One who fashioned it (wa-ma sawwaha), and He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety. Some people say that it is eternal and has no originator; others say rather that it is the one that originates its own wickedness and piety. So He, glorified is He, mentioned that He is the One who fashioned it and originated it, and that He is the One who inspired it with wickedness and piety. Thus He informed us that He is the Creator of souls and their deeds. He mentioned the word "fashioning" (taswiyah) as He mentioned it in His saying ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous, who created you and proportioned you and balanced you?﴾ and in His saying ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾, as an indication that the body is included in the word "soul," as in His saying ﴿He it is who created you from one soul﴾, and His saying ﴿So greet one another with a greeting from Allah﴾ [literally: "greet yourselves"] ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of their own kind?﴾ and its like. (Section)

He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And by the soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾

He informed that He proportioned the soul just as He informed that He proportioned the body in His saying: ﴿Who created you and proportioned you and balanced you﴾.

So He, glorified is He, proportioned the human soul just as He proportioned his body; rather, He proportioned his body as the heart is to its soul. The proportioning of the body follows the proportioning of the soul, and the body is established for it as the heart is established for what it is established for.

From here it is known that the soul takes from its body a form by which it is distinguished from others, for it is affected and moves away from the body, just as the body is affected and moves away from it. So the body acquires good and evil from the goodness and evil of the soul, and the soul acquires good and evil from the goodness and evil of the body. Of all things, the most closely bound, proportionate, interactive and affected by one another are the spirit and the body.

For this reason it is said at the time of departure: "Come out, O good soul, which was in a good body; come out, O evil soul, which was in an evil body."

(Section)

Among that is His, the Exalted, informing that He is the One who inspires His servant with his wickedness and his piety. Inspiration (al-ilham) is casting into the heart, not merely clarifying and teaching, as a group of the exegetes said; for one does not say of someone who explained to another and taught him something that he has inspired him with that. This is not known in the language at all. Rather, the correct view is what Ibn Zayd said: he said, "He placed in it its wickedness and its piety." And upon this is the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn:

"That a man from Muzaynah or Juhaynah came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you see what people do and strive for: is it something decreed for them and passed upon them from a previous destiny, or is it about what they will face from what their Prophet has brought them?'

He said: 'Rather, it is something decreed for them and passed.'

He said: 'Then what is the point of action?' He said: 'Whoever Allah has created for one of the two abodes, He makes him act by the deeds of its people.' And the confirmation of this is in the Book of Allah: ﴿And by the soul and He who proportioned it. And inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾."

His recitation of this verse following his mention of the prior decree and destiny indicates that the meaning of inspiration is directing it toward what was previously determined for it, not merely making it known, for mere informing and clarifying do not necessitate the occurrence of what was decreed in advance. And whoever among the early scholars interpreted the verse as teaching and informing, his meaning is an informing that necessitates the occurrence of that, not a bare informing detached from occurrence, for that is not called inspiration. And with Allah is success.

(Rule: When those who reason and other than them are gathered together, those who reason take precedence)

He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Among them is he who walks on his belly﴾, and likewise ﴿on four﴾, which indicates the use of (man, "who") for those who do not reason.

There are two aspects to this:

First: the beginning of the verse is His saying: ﴿And Allah created every creature from water﴾.

So all creatures were gathered together, including those who reason, such as humans, and those who do not reason, such as animals.

The rule is: when those who reason and others are gathered together, those who reason take precedence. So when the detail came, it was a detail of the rational ones only.

The second aspect: it corresponds to "he who walks" in His saying: ﴿Among them is he who walks on two legs﴾, so He departed from the original usage for the sake of the required correspondence.

It has also been said that (ma, "what") is also used for those who reason, as in His saying:

It was answered that (ma) here is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), its meaning being: "Nor are you worshippers of my worship, nor am I a worshipper of your worship." So (ma) is used only for what does not reason.

Likewise they answered regarding His saying: ﴿And by the soul and He who proportioned it﴾, except that a difficulty arose for them concerning the pronoun in His saying: ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾, since (ma) as a verbal-noun particle is a letter to which pronouns do not refer.

Some of them accepted the pronoun's referring back to it, namely the verbal-noun (ma), but this is weak.

Among what has been given a strained interpretation is His saying: ﴿And by Him who created the male and the female﴾.

And among what is difficult to interpret is His saying: ﴿So marry what is lawful to you of women﴾.

And women reason.

The Shaykh said: I say: Abu al-Baqa' and others mentioned that it was only said ﴿and the soul and He who proportioned it﴾ because "who" (man) is not used for what does not reason, and Allah is not described with this expression; rather He is described with knowledge. So (ma), which denotes the named thing, was used: "He who proportioned it."

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 91, verses 9–10 (part 1 of 2)**

The meaning: He has succeeded who makes it great and exalted by obeying Allah, and makes it manifest. He has failed and lost who conceals it, belittles it, and diminishes it through disobedience to Allah.

The root of *tadsiyah* (concealment, burying) is hiding. From it is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Or does he bury it in the dust?﴾

So the disobedient person buries his soul through disobedience and hides its place. He conceals himself from the creation because of the evil he commits. He is humbled in his own eyes, humbled before Allah, and humbled before the creation.

As for obedience and righteousness, they make the soul great, strengthen it, and raise it, until it becomes the most noble and greatest of things, the purest and highest of things. Yet, with all of that, it is the most humble, lowliest, and smallest of things before Allah, Exalted is He. Through this humility before Allah, the soul attains this might, nobility, and growth. Nothing diminishes souls like disobedience to Allah, and nothing makes them great, ennobles them, and raises them like obedience to Allah.

He said in *al-Fawaid*:

"If the soul were noble and great, it would not be content with the base. The root of all good is by the grace of Allah and His will, and the nobility, honour, and greatness of the soul. The root of all evil is its baseness, lowliness, and smallness." Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who buries it.﴾

That is: he has succeeded who makes it great, increases it, and causes it to grow through obedience to Allah, and he has failed who diminishes it and belittles it through the disobedience of Allah. Noble souls are not content with anything except its highest and best, and that which has the best outcome. Base souls hover around vileness and settle upon it, as flies settle upon filth. The noble, elevated soul is not content with injustice, with indecencies, with theft, or with betrayal, because it is greater and more exalted than that. The contemptible, despicable, and base soul is the opposite of that. Every soul inclines toward what suits it and resembles it, and this is the meaning of the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Each acts according to his manner (shakilah)."﴾

That is, according to what resembles it and suits it.

He said in *Ighathat al-Lahfan*:

The saying of Allah: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ is in the same manner as His saying: ﴿Would you have a desire to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:18]

That is, that you act in obedience to Allah, so you become pure. Similar is His saying: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾ [al-A'la 87:14].

There is a difference of opinion about the pronoun in His saying *zakkaha* (He purifies it). It was said: it refers to Allah. That is, the soul that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, purifies has succeeded, and the soul that He buries has failed.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the subject of *aflaha* (has succeeded), which is *man* (he who), whether it is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. For if the pronoun referred to Allah, Subhanahu, it would say: "He has succeeded who purified him and he has failed who buried him."

The first group says: *man*, though its form is masculine, when it refers to a feminine noun, it is permissible to refer back to it with a feminine pronoun, observing the meaning, and with a masculine pronoun, observing the form. Both are eloquent speech.

Both considerations occur in the Qur'an. The first (observing the form) is like His saying: ﴿And among them is he who listens to you﴾ [al-An'am 6:25], where the pronoun is singular. The second (observing the meaning) is like His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [Yunus 10:42], where the pronoun is plural.

Those who favour the first view say: what supports our position is what the compilers of the Sunan narrated from the hadith of Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said:

"One night I came and found the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saying: 'My Lord, give my soul its piety, and purify it, for You are the best to purify it. You are its Guardian and its Master.'"

This supplication is like an explanation of this verse, and that Allah, Exalted is He, is the one who purifies souls so that they become pure. So Allah is the one who purifies (*al-muzakki*), and the servant is the one who purifies himself (*al-mutazakki*).

The difference between them is the difference between the agent and the one affected by the action (*al-fa'il* and *al-mutawa'*).

They said: what has come in the Qur'an attributing purification to the servant is only in the second sense, not the first. Such as His saying: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾ and His saying: ﴿Would you have a desire to purify yourself?﴾

That is, that you accept the purification of Allah, Exalted is He, for you, so that you become purified? They said: and this is the truth, for none succeeds except the one whom Allah purifies. They said: and this is the preference of the interpreter of the Qur'an, Ibn Abbas, for he said in the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah, Ata', and al-Kalbi:

"He has succeeded who whose soul Allah has purified."

Ibn Zayd said: "He has succeeded who whose soul Allah has purified."

Ibn Jarir also chose this view.

They said: what supports this view also is His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ [al-Shams 91:8].

They said: and also, He, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, informed that He is the Creator of the soul and its attributes, and that is in the sense of *taswiyah* (proportioning/forming).

The proponents of the other view said: the apparent meaning of the speech and its correct construction require that the pronoun refer to *man*, that is: he has succeeded who purifies his own soul.

This is the meaning that comes immediately to understanding, and indeed one can hardly understand anything else, as when you say: "This is a slave-girl, whoever buys her has profited," "This is a prayer, whoever prays it has been made happy," "This is a lost thing, whoever shelters it has failed," and similar examples.

They said: and the soul is feminine. So if the pronoun referred to Allah, Subhanahu, the expression would be: "The soul that He purified has succeeded," or "She who He purified has succeeded," since *man* refers to the soul.

They said: even if it is permissible to leave the verb without the feminine marker for the sake of the form of *man*, as you say: "He has succeeded who among you women stood," that is when no confusion or ambiguity arises. When confusion arises, there is no alternative to mentioning what removes it.

They said: and *man* is a relative pronoun meaning *alladhi* (the one who). If it were said: "He has succeeded whom Allah purified," it would not be permissible, because the feminine pronoun would refer back to *alladhi*, which is masculine.

They said: and He, Subhanahu, intended to attribute success to the owner of the soul when he purifies his soul. For this reason the verb is left without the feminine marker, and He used *man*, which means *alladhi*. This is the view held by the majority of the exegetes, including the companions of Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). Qatadah said regarding ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams 91:9]:

"Whoever does good purifies it by obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

He also said: "He has succeeded who purifies his soul by righteous deeds."

Al-Hasan said: "He has succeeded who purifies his soul, sets it right, and directs it to the obedience of Allah, Exalted is He. And he has failed who destroys it and directs it to the disobedience of Allah, Exalted is He." Ibn Qutaybah said: "He means: he has succeeded who purifies his soul, that is, causes it to grow and raises it through obedience, righteousness, charity, and doing good."

﴿And he has failed who buries it﴾ [al-Shams 91:10].

That is, he diminishes it and conceals it by abandoning righteous deeds and committing sins. The immoral person is always hidden in place, weak in manliness, obscure in person, and downcast of head. So the one who commits indecencies buries his soul and suppresses it, while the one who does good raises his soul and exalts it.

The generous Arabs used to descend upon the hills and high ground so that their places would be made known to the needy seekers, and they would kindle fires at night for the travellers. The stingy used to descend into hollows, edges, and low lands, so that their places would be hidden from those who sought them. Those [the generous] raised their souls and purified them, while these [the stingy] concealed their souls and buried them. And a poet recited:

"The gatekeeper of your house, in a conspicuous place, spacious in its dwelling and its open space,
You have spared the seekers of charity the pursuit of hospitality, and the barking of dogs for one who seeks it."

These are two well-known views regarding the verse.

There is a third view: that the meaning is: he has failed who buries himself among the righteous while he is not one of them. This was related by al-Wahidi, who said: the meaning of this is that he hides himself among the righteous, so that people think he is one of them, while he is inwardly different from what the righteous are inwardly.

This, although it is true in itself, is questionable as to whether it is the intended meaning of the verse. It enters the verse only by way of generality. For one who buries his soul with immorality, when he mixes with the people of goodness, buries himself among them. And Allah, Exalted is He, knows best.

He said in *al-Tibyan*:

As for His saying: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾, the pronoun in *zakkaha* is in the nominative and refers back to *man*, and likewise in *dassaha*. The meaning is: he has succeeded who purifies himself, and he has failed who buries it.

This view is the correct one, and it is similar to His saying: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾.

When He, Subhanahu, mentions success, He ties it to the action of the one who succeeds, such as His saying: ﴿The believers have succeeded, those who in their prayer are humble﴾ up to the end of the verses.

And His saying: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them, and those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain. Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾.

And His saying: ﴿The saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is only that they say: "We hear and we obey." And those are the successful﴾.

And their likes.

Al-Hasan said: "He has succeeded who purifies himself and directs it to the obedience of Allah, and he has failed who destroys it and directs it to the disobedience of Allah." Qatadah said the same.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "He means: he has succeeded who purifies himself, that is, causes it to grow and raises it through obedience, righteousness, charity, and doing good. And he has failed who buries it, that is, diminishes it and conceals it by abandoning righteous deeds and committing sins. The immoral person is always hidden in place, weak in manliness, obscure in person, and downcast of head. So it is as if one characterized by committing indecencies buried himself and suppressed himself, while the one who does good made himself famous and raised himself."

Abu al-Abbas said: I asked Ibn al-A'rabi about His saying: ﴿and he has failed who buries it﴾, and he said: *dassa* means he buried himself among the righteous while he is not one of them. On this basis, the meaning is: he hid himself among the righteous, so that people think he is one of them, while he is inwardly different from what the righteous are inwardly.

Another group said: the pronoun refers back to Allah, Subhanahu. Ibn Abbas said in the narration of Ata': "The soul that Allah purified and set right has succeeded."

This is the view of Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Kalbi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Muqatil. They said: "A soul has been made happy, and a soul has succeeded whom Allah set right, purified, and enabled to obey until it acted upon it. And a soul has failed and lost whom Allah led astray, misguided, nullified, and destroyed."

The proponents of this view said: Allah has sworn by these things He mentioned because they indicate His oneness, and indicate the success of the one He purifies and the loss of the one He forsakes, so that no one thinks that he himself is the one who purifies his soul or destroys it through sin without a prior decree and an earlier determination. They said: this is more eloquent regarding the monotheism for which this surah was revealed. They said: and it is supported by His saying: ﴿And inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾.

They said: it is also supported by the hadith of Nafi', from Ibn Umar, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), that she said: "My soul awoke one night, and I found the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saying: 'My Lord, give my soul its piety, and purify it, You are the best to purify it, You are its Guardian and its Master.'" They said: this supplication is the interpretation of the verse, by the evidence of another hadith, that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he recited ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾, would pause and then say: "O Allah, grant my soul its piety. You are its Guardian and its Master. Purify it, for You are the best to purify it." They said: and in this is what clarifies that the whole matter belongs to Him, Subhanahu, for He is the Creator of the soul, the One who inspires it with wickedness and piety, and He is the one who purifies it and buries it. So the servant has no share in the matter, and he possesses nothing of the command of his own soul.

The proponents of the first view said: this view, although it is permissible in Arabic, carries the object pronoun according to the meaning of *man*, even though its form is masculine, as in His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾, where the pronoun is plural, and the form of *man* is singular, following its meaning. This is good only where no ambiguity arises regarding the referent of the pronouns. Here, the word *man* has already occurred, and the nominative pronoun in *zakkaha* rightly belongs to it in both form and meaning, so it has the better claim to it.

Then the object pronoun refers back to the soul, which has the better claim to it in both form and meaning. This is the natural arrangement required by the context of the speech and its structure. As for referring the pronoun that immediately follows *man* back to the earlier relative clause, which is His saying: ﴿And by the soul and Him who proportioned it﴾, and leaving aside its adjacent neighbour, which is *man*, and then referring the object pronoun, which is feminine, back to *man* whose form is masculine, rather than to the feminine soul, this would be permissible only if the speech had no other more fitting interpretation. But when the context and structure of the speech require otherwise, and there is no necessity for it, then interpreting it in that way is impermissible.

They said: the view we have mentioned is more preferable in meaning, for several reasons:

The first: it contains an indication of what preceded, namely the tying of success to the action and choice of the servant, as is the method of the Qur'an.

The second: it contains an additional benefit, which is the affirmation of the servant's action, his acquisition, and what he is rewarded or punished for.

In His saying: ﴿And inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ is the affirmation of the decree and the prior determination. Thus the two verses contain these two great foundations, which often occur together in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a reminder; so whoever wills may remember it. And they will not remember except that Allah wills﴾, and His saying: ﴿For whoever among you wills to be upright. And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Thus the two verses contain a refutation of both the Qadariyyah and the Jabriyyah.

The third: our view entails your view, but not vice versa. For when the servant purifies his soul and buries it, he purifies it after Allah has purified it by His guidance and help, and he buries it after Allah has buried it by forsaking him and leaving him to himself. By contrast, if the meaning were based on pure prior determination, there would be no mention at all of the servant's acquisition and action here.

[Section: Sins Diminish the Soul]

Among their punishments is that they diminish the soul, suppress it, bury it, and belittle it, until it becomes the smallest and most contemptible of all things, just as obedience causes it to grow, purifies it, and makes it great. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who buries it﴾ [al-Shams 91:9–10].

The meaning is: he has succeeded who makes it great and exalts it through obedience to Allah and makes it manifest, and he has lost who conceals it, belittles it, and diminishes it through disobedience to Allah.

The root of *tadsiyah* is concealment, and from it is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Or does he bury it in the dust?﴾ [al-Nahl 16:59].

So the disobedient person buries his soul in disobedience and hides its place. He hides from the creation because of the evil he commits. He is humbled in his own eyes, humbled before Allah, and humbled before the creation. As for obedience and righteousness, they make the soul great, strengthen it, and raise it, until it becomes the most noble and greatest of things, the purest and highest of things. Yet, with all of that, it is the most humble, lowliest, and smallest of things before Allah, Exalted is He. Through this humility before Allah, it attains this might, nobility, and growth. Nothing diminishes souls like disobedience to Allah, and nothing makes them great, ennobles them, and raises them like obedience to Allah.

(Chapter)

The reality of *adab* (good manners, refinement) is the practice of beautiful character. For this reason, *adab* is the drawing out of the perfection that is in the nature from potential into actuality.

Indeed, Allah, Subhanahu, prepared man to accept perfection by what He gave him of capacity and readiness, which He placed within him latent like fire in flint.

He inspired him, enabled him, made him know, and guided him. He sent His messengers to him and sent down His books to him, to draw out that potential by which He qualified him for his perfection into actuality.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And by the soul and Him who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety. He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who buries it﴾ [al-Shams 91:7–10].

He expressed the character of the soul by *taswiyah* (proportioning) to indicate balance and completeness. Then He informed of its acceptance of wickedness and piety, and that this came to it from Him as a test and trial. Then He singled out for success the one who purifies it, so He causes it to grow and raises it. He elevates it with His manners, with which He trained His messengers, prophets, and friends, which is piety. Then He decreed misery upon the one who buries it, so He hides it, belittles it, diminishes it, and suppresses it with wickedness. And Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, knows best.

[Section: The Ninth Station, the Station of Inspiration]

[Inspiration is the station of those who are spoken to (muhaddathun)]

Section: The Ninth Station, the Station of Inspiration.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And by the soul and Him who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ [al-Shams 91:7].

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 91, verse 9–10 (part 2 of 2):

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Husayn ibn Mundhir al-Khuza'i, when he embraced Islam: "Say: O Allah, inspire me with my right guidance, and protect me from the evil of my soul."

The author of al-Manazil (Sahib al-Manazil, i.e., Abu Isma'il al-Ansari) made inspiration (al-ilham) the station of those who are spoken to (al-muhaddathun), and he said: it is above the station of firasa (discernment), because firasa may occur rarely and may be difficult for its possessor at times, or may disobey him, whereas inspiration only occurs in a ready station.

I say: tahdith is more specific than ilham. Ilham is general among the believers according to their faith: every believer has been inspired by Allah with the guidance through which faith came to him. As for tahdith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said about it: "If there is among this Ummah anyone (spoken to), it is 'Umar," meaning among the muhaddathun. So tahdith is a specific inspiration, and it is revelation (wahy) to other than the prophets, either to those who are responsible (mukallafun), as in His saying, ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Musa, "Suckle him"﴾ [al-Qasas: 7], and His saying, ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples, "Believe in Me and My Messenger"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 111];

or to those who are not responsible, as in His saying, ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee, "Take for yourself houses in the mountains and in the trees and in what they construct"﴾ [al-Nahl: 68]. All of this is the revelation of ilham.

As for his placing it above the station of firasa, it has been objected to on the ground that firasa may occur rarely, as has already been mentioned, and the rare has no ruling; and it may disobey its possessor and be difficult for him so that it does not comply with him, whereas ilham only occurs in a ready station, meaning in the station of nearness and presence.

The verification of this matter is that each of "firasa" and "ilham" is divided into general and specific; the specific of each of them is above the general of the other; the general of each may occur frequently, and its specific may occur rarely. But the correct distinction is that firasa may be connected with a kind of acquisition and attainment, whereas ilham is a bare gift, not attained by acquisition at all.

[Chapter: The Degrees of Ilham]
[The First Degree: a report that occurs as decisive revelation accompanied by hearing]

Chapter: The degrees of ilham.

He said: it is of three degrees:

The first degree: a report (naba') that occurs as decisive revelation accompanied by hearing, since the absolute meaning of naba' is a news that has significance; not every news is a naba'. It is a report of news about a great unseen matter.

By revelation and ilham he means the information which binds whoever receives it by its necessity, either through the medium of hearing, or it is information without a medium.

I say: as for its occurrence through the medium of hearing, that is not ilham; rather it is of the category of direct address (khitab), and this is impossible to occur to other than the prophets, and it is what was specifically granted to Musa, since the one addressing him was the Truth, Mighty and Majestic.

As for what occurs to many of the practitioners of spiritual exercises (arbab al-riyadat) of hearing, it is from one of three aspects with no fourth: the highest of them is that an angel addresses him with a particular address; this occurs to others than the prophets. The angels used to greet 'Imran ibn Husayn with peace, and when he cauterized himself, they stopped addressing him, and when he left off cauterization, the angelic address returned to him. This is of two kinds:

One of them: an address he hears with his ear, and this is rare relative to the generality of believers.

The second: an address cast into his heart, by which the angel addresses his spirit, as in the well-known hadith: "Indeed the angel has a whisper (lamma) in the heart of the son of Adam, and Satan has a whisper. The whisper of the angel is a promise of good and affirmation of the truth; the whisper of Satan is a promise of evil and denial of the truth." Then he recited, ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to indecency, but Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268]. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. It was said in its interpretation: strengthen their hearts and give them good news of victory; and it was said: be present with them in the fighting. Both sayings are true, for they were present with them in the fighting and strengthened their hearts.

From this kind of address is the admonisher of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the hearts of His believing servants, as in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi and the Musnad of Ahmad, from the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Allah has struck a parable: a straight path, and on either side of the path are two walls, which have open doors, and over the doors are hanging curtains; and a caller calls from the head of the path, and a caller calls from above the path. The straight path is Islam, the two walls are the limits of Allah, the open doors are the prohibitions of Allah; no one falls into a limit of Allah's limits until he uncovers the curtain. The caller at the head of the path is the Book of Allah, and the caller above the path is the admonisher of Allah in the heart of every believer." This admonisher in the hearts of the believers is the divine ilham through the medium of the angels.

As for its occurrence without a medium, that has not yet been made clear, and a definite affirmation or negation of it depends on evidence. And Allah knows best.

(Chapter)
The second type of heard address: the voices (hawatif) of the jinn. The addresser may be a righteous believing jinn, and may be a devil (shaytan). This too is of two kinds:

One of them: that he addresses him with an address he hears with his ear.

The second: that he casts into his heart when he approaches him, and of it is his promise and wishful thinking when he promises the human and beguiles him, and orders him and forbids him, as Allah, Exalted, said, ﴿He promises them and beguiles them, and what Satan promises them is only delusion﴾ [al-Nisa': 120]. And He said, ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to indecency﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268].

The heart has a share in this address, and the ear also has a share in it; infallibility is absent except for the messengers and the consensus of the Ummah (majma' al-ummah).

So from where does the one addressed know that this address is from the Merciful or from an angel? By what proof? By what evidence? Satan casts his revelation into the soul and throws his address into the hearing, and the deceived, beguiled person says: "I was told and I was addressed." You are right, but the matter lies with the one who speaks to you and the one who addresses you. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Ghaylan ibn Salamah, who was a Companion, when he divorced his wives and divided his wealth among his sons: "I think that Satan, in what he steals by eavesdropping, heard of your death and cast it into your soul." Then, "Who will be safe from the reciters after you, O Shahr?"

(Chapter)
The third type: a present (hali) address, whose beginning is from the self and whose return is to it, so he imagines it comes from outside, while it is only from his own self; it begins from it and returns to it.

This often befalls the wayfarer (salik), and he errs in it and believes it is an address from Allah, which He spoke to him from Himself to Himself. The cause of his error is that the perceptive subtle faculty of the human, when it is purified by spiritual exercise and its ties are cut off from dense preoccupations, the judgment becomes its, by the rule of the spirit and heart dominating the body, and the judgment reverts to them; so the attention of the self and heart turns to stripping away the meanings that are connected to them, the attention of the spirit intensifies on them, and it comes to occupy the place of those ties and preoccupations, so it fills the heart; then those meanings turn into speech and inner spiritual address by habit. The spirit happens to become detached, so those meanings take the form, for the hearing faculty, of audible voices, and for the seeing faculty, of visible figures, so he sees their images and hears the address, and all of it is in his self, nothing of it is outside. He swears that he saw and heard, and he is sincere; but did he see and hear outside, or in his self?

Weakness of discernment, scarcity of knowledge, and the dominance of those meanings over the spirit, and its detachment from preoccupations, happen together.

These three aspects are the aspects of address. Whoever hears his self in other than them, that is only delusion, deception and misleading. This point is the end of the discussion, and it is among the most important places for whoever verifies and understands it. And Allah is the Granter of success to what is right.

[Chapter: The Second Degree: ilham that occurs as direct witnessing]

He said: "The second degree: ilham that occurs as direct witnessing (iyanan), and the sign of its soundness is that it does not tear a veil, nor exceed a limit, and it never errs."

The difference between this and ilham in the first degree is that that is a knowledge akin to the necessary, which cannot be repelled from the heart, whereas this is direct observation and unveiling (mu'ayanah wa mukashafah). So it is above it in degree and more complete in manifestation; its relation to the heart is the relation of the seen to the eye. He mentioned three signs for it:

The first: that it does not tear a veil, i.e., its possessor, when unveiled to a state of what is not concealed from him, does not tear its veil and expose it, whether good or evil; or that it does not tear what Allah has concealed of himself from people, but he conceals himself and conceals the one whose state has been unveiled to him.

The second: that it does not exceed a limit, which may bear two meanings:

One of them: that it does not carry him beyond to committing sins and transgressing the limits of Allah, like the soothsayers and the possessors of satanic unveiling.

The second: that it does not occur contrary to the legal limits, such as spying through it on the private matters (awrat) which Allah has forbidden spying upon and pursuing. If he pursues them and reaches them through this unveiling, then it is satanic, not merciful.

The third: that it never errs, unlike the satanic, whose errors are many. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ibn Sayyad: "What do you see?" He said: "I see a truthful one and a liar." He said: "You have been confused." So satanic unveiling must lie, and its truthfulness never continues at all.

[Chapter: The Third Degree: ilham that purely illuminates the eye of verification]

He said: "The third degree: ilham that purely illuminates the eye of verification, and speaks purely from the eye of the Eternal, and ilham is an ultimate state to which pointing is impossible."

The eye of verification, according to him, is annihilation (fana') in the witnessing of the Reality, such that everything else dissolves in that witnessing, and the traces become pure nonexistence. So ilham in this degree purely illuminates this eye for the one inspired, such that nothing of the perception of intellects or senses mixes with it; if there is any rational or sensory perception there, the illumination of the eye of Reality is not pure. The one who speaks of this unveiling among them is understood only by one who is with him and shares with him. According to the people of this unveiling, all creation is in a veil from it; they hold that knowledge, intellect and state are veils over it, that the address of creatures is only through the tongue of the veil, and that they do not understand the language of what lies behind the veil of the hidden meaning. Therefore pointing to it and expressing it are impossible, for pointing and expression only relate to the sensible and the intelligible, and this is a matter beyond sense and intellect.

The outcome of this ilham is that it is an ilham in which intermediaries are lifted, dissolve and cease to be, but in witnessing, not in existence. As for the monists (al-ittihadiyyah), who hold the unity of existence (wahdat al-wujud), they make that a dissolution and nonexistence in existence itself, and they count the author of al-Manazil among them, though he is innocent of them in intellect, religion, state and knowledge. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 91, verses 9–10 (part 1 of 2)**

The meaning: He has succeeded who makes it great and exalted by obeying Allah, and makes it manifest. He has failed and lost who conceals it, belittles it, and diminishes it through disobedience to Allah.

The root of *tadsiyah* (concealment, burying) is hiding. From it is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Or does he bury it in the dust?﴾

So the disobedient person buries his soul through disobedience and hides its place. He conceals himself from the creation because of the evil he commits. He is humbled in his own eyes, humbled before Allah, and humbled before the creation.

As for obedience and righteousness, they make the soul great, strengthen it, and raise it, until it becomes the most noble and greatest of things, the purest and highest of things. Yet, with all of that, it is the most humble, lowliest, and smallest of things before Allah, Exalted is He. Through this humility before Allah, the soul attains this might, nobility, and growth. Nothing diminishes souls like disobedience to Allah, and nothing makes them great, ennobles them, and raises them like obedience to Allah.

He said in *al-Fawaid*:

"If the soul were noble and great, it would not be content with the base. The root of all good is by the grace of Allah and His will, and the nobility, honour, and greatness of the soul. The root of all evil is its baseness, lowliness, and smallness." Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who buries it.﴾

That is: he has succeeded who makes it great, increases it, and causes it to grow through obedience to Allah, and he has failed who diminishes it and belittles it through the disobedience of Allah. Noble souls are not content with anything except its highest and best, and that which has the best outcome. Base souls hover around vileness and settle upon it, as flies settle upon filth. The noble, elevated soul is not content with injustice, with indecencies, with theft, or with betrayal, because it is greater and more exalted than that. The contemptible, despicable, and base soul is the opposite of that. Every soul inclines toward what suits it and resembles it, and this is the meaning of the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Each acts according to his manner (shakilah)."﴾

That is, according to what resembles it and suits it.

He said in *Ighathat al-Lahfan*:

The saying of Allah: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ is in the same manner as His saying: ﴿Would you have a desire to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:18]

That is, that you act in obedience to Allah, so you become pure. Similar is His saying: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾ [al-A'la 87:14].

There is a difference of opinion about the pronoun in His saying *zakkaha* (He purifies it). It was said: it refers to Allah. That is, the soul that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, purifies has succeeded, and the soul that He buries has failed.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the subject of *aflaha* (has succeeded), which is *man* (he who), whether it is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. For if the pronoun referred to Allah, Subhanahu, it would say: "He has succeeded who purified him and he has failed who buried him."

The first group says: *man*, though its form is masculine, when it refers to a feminine noun, it is permissible to refer back to it with a feminine pronoun, observing the meaning, and with a masculine pronoun, observing the form. Both are eloquent speech.

Both considerations occur in the Qur'an. The first (observing the form) is like His saying: ﴿And among them is he who listens to you﴾ [al-An'am 6:25], where the pronoun is singular. The second (observing the meaning) is like His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [Yunus 10:42], where the pronoun is plural.

Those who favour the first view say: what supports our position is what the compilers of the Sunan narrated from the hadith of Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said:

"One night I came and found the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saying: 'My Lord, give my soul its piety, and purify it, for You are the best to purify it. You are its Guardian and its Master.'"

This supplication is like an explanation of this verse, and that Allah, Exalted is He, is the one who purifies souls so that they become pure. So Allah is the one who purifies (*al-muzakki*), and the servant is the one who purifies himself (*al-mutazakki*).

The difference between them is the difference between the agent and the one affected by the action (*al-fa'il* and *al-mutawa'*).

They said: what has come in the Qur'an attributing purification to the servant is only in the second sense, not the first. Such as His saying: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾ and His saying: ﴿Would you have a desire to purify yourself?﴾

That is, that you accept the purification of Allah, Exalted is He, for you, so that you become purified? They said: and this is the truth, for none succeeds except the one whom Allah purifies. They said: and this is the preference of the interpreter of the Qur'an, Ibn Abbas, for he said in the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah, Ata', and al-Kalbi:

"He has succeeded who whose soul Allah has purified."

Ibn Zayd said: "He has succeeded who whose soul Allah has purified."

Ibn Jarir also chose this view.

They said: what supports this view also is His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ [al-Shams 91:8].

They said: and also, He, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, informed that He is the Creator of the soul and its attributes, and that is in the sense of *taswiyah* (proportioning/forming).

The proponents of the other view said: the apparent meaning of the speech and its correct construction require that the pronoun refer to *man*, that is: he has succeeded who purifies his own soul.

This is the meaning that comes immediately to understanding, and indeed one can hardly understand anything else, as when you say: "This is a slave-girl, whoever buys her has profited," "This is a prayer, whoever prays it has been made happy," "This is a lost thing, whoever shelters it has failed," and similar examples.

They said: and the soul is feminine. So if the pronoun referred to Allah, Subhanahu, the expression would be: "The soul that He purified has succeeded," or "She who He purified has succeeded," since *man* refers to the soul.

They said: even if it is permissible to leave the verb without the feminine marker for the sake of the form of *man*, as you say: "He has succeeded who among you women stood," that is when no confusion or ambiguity arises. When confusion arises, there is no alternative to mentioning what removes it.

They said: and *man* is a relative pronoun meaning *alladhi* (the one who). If it were said: "He has succeeded whom Allah purified," it would not be permissible, because the feminine pronoun would refer back to *alladhi*, which is masculine.

They said: and He, Subhanahu, intended to attribute success to the owner of the soul when he purifies his soul. For this reason the verb is left without the feminine marker, and He used *man*, which means *alladhi*. This is the view held by the majority of the exegetes, including the companions of Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). Qatadah said regarding ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams 91:9]:

"Whoever does good purifies it by obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

He also said: "He has succeeded who purifies his soul by righteous deeds."

Al-Hasan said: "He has succeeded who purifies his soul, sets it right, and directs it to the obedience of Allah, Exalted is He. And he has failed who destroys it and directs it to the disobedience of Allah, Exalted is He." Ibn Qutaybah said: "He means: he has succeeded who purifies his soul, that is, causes it to grow and raises it through obedience, righteousness, charity, and doing good."

﴿And he has failed who buries it﴾ [al-Shams 91:10].

That is, he diminishes it and conceals it by abandoning righteous deeds and committing sins. The immoral person is always hidden in place, weak in manliness, obscure in person, and downcast of head. So the one who commits indecencies buries his soul and suppresses it, while the one who does good raises his soul and exalts it.

The generous Arabs used to descend upon the hills and high ground so that their places would be made known to the needy seekers, and they would kindle fires at night for the travellers. The stingy used to descend into hollows, edges, and low lands, so that their places would be hidden from those who sought them. Those [the generous] raised their souls and purified them, while these [the stingy] concealed their souls and buried them. And a poet recited:

"The gatekeeper of your house, in a conspicuous place, spacious in its dwelling and its open space,
You have spared the seekers of charity the pursuit of hospitality, and the barking of dogs for one who seeks it."

These are two well-known views regarding the verse.

There is a third view: that the meaning is: he has failed who buries himself among the righteous while he is not one of them. This was related by al-Wahidi, who said: the meaning of this is that he hides himself among the righteous, so that people think he is one of them, while he is inwardly different from what the righteous are inwardly.

This, although it is true in itself, is questionable as to whether it is the intended meaning of the verse. It enters the verse only by way of generality. For one who buries his soul with immorality, when he mixes with the people of goodness, buries himself among them. And Allah, Exalted is He, knows best.

He said in *al-Tibyan*:

As for His saying: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾, the pronoun in *zakkaha* is in the nominative and refers back to *man*, and likewise in *dassaha*. The meaning is: he has succeeded who purifies himself, and he has failed who buries it.

This view is the correct one, and it is similar to His saying: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾.

When He, Subhanahu, mentions success, He ties it to the action of the one who succeeds, such as His saying: ﴿The believers have succeeded, those who in their prayer are humble﴾ up to the end of the verses.

And His saying: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them, and those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain. Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾.

And His saying: ﴿The saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is only that they say: "We hear and we obey." And those are the successful﴾.

And their likes.

Al-Hasan said: "He has succeeded who purifies himself and directs it to the obedience of Allah, and he has failed who destroys it and directs it to the disobedience of Allah." Qatadah said the same.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "He means: he has succeeded who purifies himself, that is, causes it to grow and raises it through obedience, righteousness, charity, and doing good. And he has failed who buries it, that is, diminishes it and conceals it by abandoning righteous deeds and committing sins. The immoral person is always hidden in place, weak in manliness, obscure in person, and downcast of head. So it is as if one characterized by committing indecencies buried himself and suppressed himself, while the one who does good made himself famous and raised himself."

Abu al-Abbas said: I asked Ibn al-A'rabi about His saying: ﴿and he has failed who buries it﴾, and he said: *dassa* means he buried himself among the righteous while he is not one of them. On this basis, the meaning is: he hid himself among the righteous, so that people think he is one of them, while he is inwardly different from what the righteous are inwardly.

Another group said: the pronoun refers back to Allah, Subhanahu. Ibn Abbas said in the narration of Ata': "The soul that Allah purified and set right has succeeded."

This is the view of Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Kalbi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Muqatil. They said: "A soul has been made happy, and a soul has succeeded whom Allah set right, purified, and enabled to obey until it acted upon it. And a soul has failed and lost whom Allah led astray, misguided, nullified, and destroyed."

The proponents of this view said: Allah has sworn by these things He mentioned because they indicate His oneness, and indicate the success of the one He purifies and the loss of the one He forsakes, so that no one thinks that he himself is the one who purifies his soul or destroys it through sin without a prior decree and an earlier determination. They said: this is more eloquent regarding the monotheism for which this surah was revealed. They said: and it is supported by His saying: ﴿And inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾.

They said: it is also supported by the hadith of Nafi', from Ibn Umar, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), that she said: "My soul awoke one night, and I found the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saying: 'My Lord, give my soul its piety, and purify it, You are the best to purify it, You are its Guardian and its Master.'" They said: this supplication is the interpretation of the verse, by the evidence of another hadith, that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he recited ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾, would pause and then say: "O Allah, grant my soul its piety. You are its Guardian and its Master. Purify it, for You are the best to purify it." They said: and in this is what clarifies that the whole matter belongs to Him, Subhanahu, for He is the Creator of the soul, the One who inspires it with wickedness and piety, and He is the one who purifies it and buries it. So the servant has no share in the matter, and he possesses nothing of the command of his own soul.

The proponents of the first view said: this view, although it is permissible in Arabic, carries the object pronoun according to the meaning of *man*, even though its form is masculine, as in His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾, where the pronoun is plural, and the form of *man* is singular, following its meaning. This is good only where no ambiguity arises regarding the referent of the pronouns. Here, the word *man* has already occurred, and the nominative pronoun in *zakkaha* rightly belongs to it in both form and meaning, so it has the better claim to it.

Then the object pronoun refers back to the soul, which has the better claim to it in both form and meaning. This is the natural arrangement required by the context of the speech and its structure. As for referring the pronoun that immediately follows *man* back to the earlier relative clause, which is His saying: ﴿And by the soul and Him who proportioned it﴾, and leaving aside its adjacent neighbour, which is *man*, and then referring the object pronoun, which is feminine, back to *man* whose form is masculine, rather than to the feminine soul, this would be permissible only if the speech had no other more fitting interpretation. But when the context and structure of the speech require otherwise, and there is no necessity for it, then interpreting it in that way is impermissible.

They said: the view we have mentioned is more preferable in meaning, for several reasons:

The first: it contains an indication of what preceded, namely the tying of success to the action and choice of the servant, as is the method of the Qur'an.

The second: it contains an additional benefit, which is the affirmation of the servant's action, his acquisition, and what he is rewarded or punished for.

In His saying: ﴿And inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ is the affirmation of the decree and the prior determination. Thus the two verses contain these two great foundations, which often occur together in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a reminder; so whoever wills may remember it. And they will not remember except that Allah wills﴾, and His saying: ﴿For whoever among you wills to be upright. And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Thus the two verses contain a refutation of both the Qadariyyah and the Jabriyyah.

The third: our view entails your view, but not vice versa. For when the servant purifies his soul and buries it, he purifies it after Allah has purified it by His guidance and help, and he buries it after Allah has buried it by forsaking him and leaving him to himself. By contrast, if the meaning were based on pure prior determination, there would be no mention at all of the servant's acquisition and action here.

[Section: Sins Diminish the Soul]

Among their punishments is that they diminish the soul, suppress it, bury it, and belittle it, until it becomes the smallest and most contemptible of all things, just as obedience causes it to grow, purifies it, and makes it great. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who buries it﴾ [al-Shams 91:9–10].

The meaning is: he has succeeded who makes it great and exalts it through obedience to Allah and makes it manifest, and he has lost who conceals it, belittles it, and diminishes it through disobedience to Allah.

The root of *tadsiyah* is concealment, and from it is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Or does he bury it in the dust?﴾ [al-Nahl 16:59].

So the disobedient person buries his soul in disobedience and hides its place. He hides from the creation because of the evil he commits. He is humbled in his own eyes, humbled before Allah, and humbled before the creation. As for obedience and righteousness, they make the soul great, strengthen it, and raise it, until it becomes the most noble and greatest of things, the purest and highest of things. Yet, with all of that, it is the most humble, lowliest, and smallest of things before Allah, Exalted is He. Through this humility before Allah, it attains this might, nobility, and growth. Nothing diminishes souls like disobedience to Allah, and nothing makes them great, ennobles them, and raises them like obedience to Allah.

(Chapter)

The reality of *adab* (good manners, refinement) is the practice of beautiful character. For this reason, *adab* is the drawing out of the perfection that is in the nature from potential into actuality.

Indeed, Allah, Subhanahu, prepared man to accept perfection by what He gave him of capacity and readiness, which He placed within him latent like fire in flint.

He inspired him, enabled him, made him know, and guided him. He sent His messengers to him and sent down His books to him, to draw out that potential by which He qualified him for his perfection into actuality.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And by the soul and Him who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety. He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who buries it﴾ [al-Shams 91:7–10].

He expressed the character of the soul by *taswiyah* (proportioning) to indicate balance and completeness. Then He informed of its acceptance of wickedness and piety, and that this came to it from Him as a test and trial. Then He singled out for success the one who purifies it, so He causes it to grow and raises it. He elevates it with His manners, with which He trained His messengers, prophets, and friends, which is piety. Then He decreed misery upon the one who buries it, so He hides it, belittles it, diminishes it, and suppresses it with wickedness. And Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, knows best.

[Section: The Ninth Station, the Station of Inspiration]

[Inspiration is the station of those who are spoken to (muhaddathun)]

Section: The Ninth Station, the Station of Inspiration.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And by the soul and Him who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ [al-Shams 91:7].

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 91, verse 9–10 (part 2 of 2):

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Husayn ibn Mundhir al-Khuza'i, when he embraced Islam: "Say: O Allah, inspire me with my right guidance, and protect me from the evil of my soul."

The author of al-Manazil (Sahib al-Manazil, i.e., Abu Isma'il al-Ansari) made inspiration (al-ilham) the station of those who are spoken to (al-muhaddathun), and he said: it is above the station of firasa (discernment), because firasa may occur rarely and may be difficult for its possessor at times, or may disobey him, whereas inspiration only occurs in a ready station.

I say: tahdith is more specific than ilham. Ilham is general among the believers according to their faith: every believer has been inspired by Allah with the guidance through which faith came to him. As for tahdith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said about it: "If there is among this Ummah anyone (spoken to), it is 'Umar," meaning among the muhaddathun. So tahdith is a specific inspiration, and it is revelation (wahy) to other than the prophets, either to those who are responsible (mukallafun), as in His saying, ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Musa, "Suckle him"﴾ [al-Qasas: 7], and His saying, ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples, "Believe in Me and My Messenger"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 111];

or to those who are not responsible, as in His saying, ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee, "Take for yourself houses in the mountains and in the trees and in what they construct"﴾ [al-Nahl: 68]. All of this is the revelation of ilham.

As for his placing it above the station of firasa, it has been objected to on the ground that firasa may occur rarely, as has already been mentioned, and the rare has no ruling; and it may disobey its possessor and be difficult for him so that it does not comply with him, whereas ilham only occurs in a ready station, meaning in the station of nearness and presence.

The verification of this matter is that each of "firasa" and "ilham" is divided into general and specific; the specific of each of them is above the general of the other; the general of each may occur frequently, and its specific may occur rarely. But the correct distinction is that firasa may be connected with a kind of acquisition and attainment, whereas ilham is a bare gift, not attained by acquisition at all.

[Chapter: The Degrees of Ilham]
[The First Degree: a report that occurs as decisive revelation accompanied by hearing]

Chapter: The degrees of ilham.

He said: it is of three degrees:

The first degree: a report (naba') that occurs as decisive revelation accompanied by hearing, since the absolute meaning of naba' is a news that has significance; not every news is a naba'. It is a report of news about a great unseen matter.

By revelation and ilham he means the information which binds whoever receives it by its necessity, either through the medium of hearing, or it is information without a medium.

I say: as for its occurrence through the medium of hearing, that is not ilham; rather it is of the category of direct address (khitab), and this is impossible to occur to other than the prophets, and it is what was specifically granted to Musa, since the one addressing him was the Truth, Mighty and Majestic.

As for what occurs to many of the practitioners of spiritual exercises (arbab al-riyadat) of hearing, it is from one of three aspects with no fourth: the highest of them is that an angel addresses him with a particular address; this occurs to others than the prophets. The angels used to greet 'Imran ibn Husayn with peace, and when he cauterized himself, they stopped addressing him, and when he left off cauterization, the angelic address returned to him. This is of two kinds:

One of them: an address he hears with his ear, and this is rare relative to the generality of believers.

The second: an address cast into his heart, by which the angel addresses his spirit, as in the well-known hadith: "Indeed the angel has a whisper (lamma) in the heart of the son of Adam, and Satan has a whisper. The whisper of the angel is a promise of good and affirmation of the truth; the whisper of Satan is a promise of evil and denial of the truth." Then he recited, ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to indecency, but Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268]. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. It was said in its interpretation: strengthen their hearts and give them good news of victory; and it was said: be present with them in the fighting. Both sayings are true, for they were present with them in the fighting and strengthened their hearts.

From this kind of address is the admonisher of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the hearts of His believing servants, as in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi and the Musnad of Ahmad, from the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Allah has struck a parable: a straight path, and on either side of the path are two walls, which have open doors, and over the doors are hanging curtains; and a caller calls from the head of the path, and a caller calls from above the path. The straight path is Islam, the two walls are the limits of Allah, the open doors are the prohibitions of Allah; no one falls into a limit of Allah's limits until he uncovers the curtain. The caller at the head of the path is the Book of Allah, and the caller above the path is the admonisher of Allah in the heart of every believer." This admonisher in the hearts of the believers is the divine ilham through the medium of the angels.

As for its occurrence without a medium, that has not yet been made clear, and a definite affirmation or negation of it depends on evidence. And Allah knows best.

(Chapter)
The second type of heard address: the voices (hawatif) of the jinn. The addresser may be a righteous believing jinn, and may be a devil (shaytan). This too is of two kinds:

One of them: that he addresses him with an address he hears with his ear.

The second: that he casts into his heart when he approaches him, and of it is his promise and wishful thinking when he promises the human and beguiles him, and orders him and forbids him, as Allah, Exalted, said, ﴿He promises them and beguiles them, and what Satan promises them is only delusion﴾ [al-Nisa': 120]. And He said, ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to indecency﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268].

The heart has a share in this address, and the ear also has a share in it; infallibility is absent except for the messengers and the consensus of the Ummah (majma' al-ummah).

So from where does the one addressed know that this address is from the Merciful or from an angel? By what proof? By what evidence? Satan casts his revelation into the soul and throws his address into the hearing, and the deceived, beguiled person says: "I was told and I was addressed." You are right, but the matter lies with the one who speaks to you and the one who addresses you. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Ghaylan ibn Salamah, who was a Companion, when he divorced his wives and divided his wealth among his sons: "I think that Satan, in what he steals by eavesdropping, heard of your death and cast it into your soul." Then, "Who will be safe from the reciters after you, O Shahr?"

(Chapter)
The third type: a present (hali) address, whose beginning is from the self and whose return is to it, so he imagines it comes from outside, while it is only from his own self; it begins from it and returns to it.

This often befalls the wayfarer (salik), and he errs in it and believes it is an address from Allah, which He spoke to him from Himself to Himself. The cause of his error is that the perceptive subtle faculty of the human, when it is purified by spiritual exercise and its ties are cut off from dense preoccupations, the judgment becomes its, by the rule of the spirit and heart dominating the body, and the judgment reverts to them; so the attention of the self and heart turns to stripping away the meanings that are connected to them, the attention of the spirit intensifies on them, and it comes to occupy the place of those ties and preoccupations, so it fills the heart; then those meanings turn into speech and inner spiritual address by habit. The spirit happens to become detached, so those meanings take the form, for the hearing faculty, of audible voices, and for the seeing faculty, of visible figures, so he sees their images and hears the address, and all of it is in his self, nothing of it is outside. He swears that he saw and heard, and he is sincere; but did he see and hear outside, or in his self?

Weakness of discernment, scarcity of knowledge, and the dominance of those meanings over the spirit, and its detachment from preoccupations, happen together.

These three aspects are the aspects of address. Whoever hears his self in other than them, that is only delusion, deception and misleading. This point is the end of the discussion, and it is among the most important places for whoever verifies and understands it. And Allah is the Granter of success to what is right.

[Chapter: The Second Degree: ilham that occurs as direct witnessing]

He said: "The second degree: ilham that occurs as direct witnessing (iyanan), and the sign of its soundness is that it does not tear a veil, nor exceed a limit, and it never errs."

The difference between this and ilham in the first degree is that that is a knowledge akin to the necessary, which cannot be repelled from the heart, whereas this is direct observation and unveiling (mu'ayanah wa mukashafah). So it is above it in degree and more complete in manifestation; its relation to the heart is the relation of the seen to the eye. He mentioned three signs for it:

The first: that it does not tear a veil, i.e., its possessor, when unveiled to a state of what is not concealed from him, does not tear its veil and expose it, whether good or evil; or that it does not tear what Allah has concealed of himself from people, but he conceals himself and conceals the one whose state has been unveiled to him.

The second: that it does not exceed a limit, which may bear two meanings:

One of them: that it does not carry him beyond to committing sins and transgressing the limits of Allah, like the soothsayers and the possessors of satanic unveiling.

The second: that it does not occur contrary to the legal limits, such as spying through it on the private matters (awrat) which Allah has forbidden spying upon and pursuing. If he pursues them and reaches them through this unveiling, then it is satanic, not merciful.

The third: that it never errs, unlike the satanic, whose errors are many. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ibn Sayyad: "What do you see?" He said: "I see a truthful one and a liar." He said: "You have been confused." So satanic unveiling must lie, and its truthfulness never continues at all.

[Chapter: The Third Degree: ilham that purely illuminates the eye of verification]

He said: "The third degree: ilham that purely illuminates the eye of verification, and speaks purely from the eye of the Eternal, and ilham is an ultimate state to which pointing is impossible."

The eye of verification, according to him, is annihilation (fana') in the witnessing of the Reality, such that everything else dissolves in that witnessing, and the traces become pure nonexistence. So ilham in this degree purely illuminates this eye for the one inspired, such that nothing of the perception of intellects or senses mixes with it; if there is any rational or sensory perception there, the illumination of the eye of Reality is not pure. The one who speaks of this unveiling among them is understood only by one who is with him and shares with him. According to the people of this unveiling, all creation is in a veil from it; they hold that knowledge, intellect and state are veils over it, that the address of creatures is only through the tongue of the veil, and that they do not understand the language of what lies behind the veil of the hidden meaning. Therefore pointing to it and expressing it are impossible, for pointing and expression only relate to the sensible and the intelligible, and this is a matter beyond sense and intellect.

The outcome of this ilham is that it is an ilham in which intermediaries are lifted, dissolve and cease to be, but in witnessing, not in existence. As for the monists (al-ittihadiyyah), who hold the unity of existence (wahdat al-wujud), they make that a dissolution and nonexistence in existence itself, and they count the author of al-Manazil among them, though he is innocent of them in intellect, religion, state and knowledge. And Allah knows best.

(Fa'idah)

The mention of Thamud in this surah, to the exclusion of the other disbelieving nations, is a point worth noting.

Our shaykh said: "This, and God knows best, is by way of alerting to the higher through the lesser. Among the disbelieving nations, none was lighter in sin and punishment than they, for there is not mentioned of them such sins as are mentioned of 'Ad, Madyan, the people of Lut, and others. This is why, when He mentioned them alongside 'Ad, He said: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right, and said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? And they used to deny Our signs. And as for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾. Likewise, when He mentions them with the disbelieving nations, He does not mention of them what He mentions of those others of tyranny, arrogance and evil deeds, such as sodomy, cheating in measure and balance, and corruption in the land, as in Surah Hud, Surah al-Shu'ara' and elsewhere. Thus with the people of Lut there was, along with shirk, the commission of the abomination which they had not been preceded in; with the people of 'Ad, along with shirk, there was tyranny, arrogance, extravagance in worldly things, and severe violence; and their saying ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [is evidence of this]. With the companions of Madyan, along with shirk, there was wrongdoing in wealth; and with the people of Pharaoh, along with shirk, there was corruption in the land and haughtiness. The punishment of each nation was in accordance with its sins and crimes. The people of 'Ad were punished with the fierce, violent wind which nothing could withstand. The people of Lut were punished with kinds of punishment with which no other nation was punished; He combined for them destruction, stoning with rocks from heaven, the blinding of their eyes, and the overturning of their dwellings upon them, by making its upper part its lower part, and sinking them down to the lowest of the low. The people of Shu'ayb were punished with fire, which burned them and burned those wealths they had acquired through wrongdoing and transgression. As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the Blast, and died instantly. So if the punishment and sin of these, along with shirk, was the hamstringing of the she-camel which God had made a sign for them, then whoever violates the sanctities of God, makes light of His commands and prohibitions, hamstrings His servants and sheds their blood, will have a greater punishment. And whoever considers the conditions of the world, past and present, and what is punished of those who strive in the land with corruption, shed blood without right, stir up strife, and disdain the sanctities of God, will know that salvation in this world and the Hereafter belongs to those who believed and were God-fearing."

I say: The singling out of Thamud here, to the exclusion of others, may also suggest another meaning: that they rejected guidance after having become certain of it, and were seeing clearly through it, their hearts having been content with it and their souls awakened to it, yet they chose blindness and misguidance over it, as God says describing them: ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾, and He says ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign﴾, meaning, one that brought them insight and certainty. Although all the destroyed nations were of this condition, God did not destroy any nation except after the establishment of proof against it; but Thamud were singled out from that guidance and insight with a greater measure. This is why, when He paired them with the people of 'Ad, He said ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right, and said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾

Then He said ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾. This is why it was possible for 'Ad to be obstinate and to say to their prophet ﴿You have brought us no clear proof﴾.

That was not possible for Thamud, who had seen the clear proof with their own eyes, and it was for them like seeing the sun and moon. So they rejected guidance after its certainty and complete insight. Thus in singling them out for mention there is a warning to everyone who knows the truth and does not follow it. This is the disease of most of those who perished, and it is the most general of diseases and the most prevalent among the people of the earth. And God knows best.

He (Allah) negated from Himself the fear of the consequence of what He did in destroying His enemies, unlike the created being, for when he takes vengeance on his enemy he fears the consequence of that, either from Allah, or from those who support his enemy.

And that is impossible for Allah.

Fear entails deficiency in knowledge, power and will. For one who knows that a thing will not happen does not fear it, and one who knows that it will certainly happen may despair of escaping it and so does not fear; and if he does fear, his fear is less than the fear of one who hopes.

As for deficiency in power: one who fears a thing is one who cannot repel it from himself, so when he is certain that he is able to repel it, he does not fear it.
